nestedscales

Documentation: https://optimal2050.github.io/nestedscales/r/

nestedscales provides the machinery for describing one dimension of data at several resolutions at once, and for moving data between those resolutions by explicit rules.

Models and statistics rarely use a dimension at a single resolution. Time is needed in hours and in months, space in cities and in countries, the economy in activities and in sectors, and data usually arrives at a resolution other than the one in use. A nested scale is the record that makes the conversion possible: it lists the finest items of a dimension and how they group, step by step, into coarser ones. With that record, a table of values at one resolution is converted to any other: summed, averaged with weights, copied down, or split in proportion.

The package is the common base of timescales (calendars) and geoscales (regions), and serves any other dimension declared from a table.

What a nested scale is

One dimension, here space, described at three resolutions, and the same data at each of them:

 the scale     frame      members
               -------    -------------------------------------------------
 coarse        country    [          North          ]  [       South      ]
               region     [    N1    ]  [    N2     ]  [        S1        ]
 fine          city       [ a ]  [ b ]  [ c ]  [ d  ]  [ e ]  [ f ]  [ g  ]

 data on it               (people, moved between the frames by the rule "sum")
               -------    -------------------------------------------------
               city         3      2      5      4       6      1      7
               region          5             9                 14
               country               14                        14
  • A frame is one resolution of the dimension: country, region, city.
  • A member is one item of a frame: North, N1, a.
  • The leaves are the members of the finest frame, the cities. The scale stores one row per leaf with its member at every frame.
  • Nesting is what the boxes show: every member of a finer frame lies inside exactly one member of the coarser frame, so a value on cities has one place to go at the region and at the country.
  • The nested scale is the whole of it: the frames, their members, and which leaf belongs to which.
library(nestedscales)

places <- scale_from_leaftable(
  data.frame(
    country = c("North", "North", "North", "North", "South", "South", "South"),
    region  = c("N1", "N1", "N2", "N2", "S1", "S1", "S1"),
    city    = c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f", "g")
  ),
  frames = c("country", "region", "city"), name = "places"
)
places
#> NestedScale: places
#> Frames (3, coarsest first):
#>   - country (2)
#>     - region (3)
#>       - city (7)
#> Leaves: 7

people <- data.frame(city = c("a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f", "g"),
                     people = c(3, 2, 5, 4, 6, 1, 7))
recast_scale(people, places, source = "city", target = "region",
             rule = "sum")
#>   region people
#> 1     N1      5
#> 2     N2      9
#> 3     S1     14
recast_scale(people, places, source = "city", target = "country",
             rule = "sum")
#>   country people
#> 1   North     14
#> 2   South     14

A scale may also hold frames that do not nest in the others, such as a grouping of the same cities by river basin. Conversion always passes through the leaves, so such a frame is used in the same way.

The package defines:

  • Structure: the frames of a scale, the members at each frame, and the relations between frames (nested, crossed, uniform).
  • Transition rules between frames, chosen per value column and aware of direction: sum, weighted_mean, mean, and copy; sd for aggregation; and share or logshare for within-parent shares.
  • Operations: converting data between frames, attaching frame labels to a dataset, subsetting, combining several scales into one multi-dimensional index, clustering members into new frames, and storing data together with its scales.
  • Labels, attributes and definitions: display names for members and frames, in named variants; values that belong to a member but are not weights (the persons per household of a city, a wage per employee), resolved along the hierarchy and applied row by row; alternative spellings matched strictly; and language-neutral definition files, with a catalogue of the ones installed packages ship.
  • A link between data and scale (experimental): the code columns of a table can record which scale and frame they are on, so a conversion is refused for data of another scale.

The package is dimension-agnostic. Time and space are provided by two packages built on it, designed for optimization and simulation models, where labeled time slices and regions serve as the index sets of variables and constraints:

  • timescales: Calendar, labeled discrete time slices (hours, days, seasons, representative days).
  • geoscales: GeoScale, labeled geographical regions with geometry.

Both classes are subclasses of NestedScale. Any other dimension (industries, income brackets, technology vintages) is declared directly from a table. vignette("nestedscales") introduces the functions; the package website includes a roadmap of what is available and what is planned.

Installation

The released version is on CRAN:

install.packages("nestedscales")

The development version is on GitHub:

pak::pkg_install("optimal2050/nestedscales")

The package is pure R; its non-base runtime dependencies are dplyr, rlang, S7, vctrs and jsonlite.

A scale in one call

Declare the frames, coarsest first:

library(nestedscales)

industries <- data.frame(
  section  = c("C", "C", "C", "D", "D"),
  division = c("C10", "C10", "C11", "D35", "D35"),
  class    = c("C101", "C102", "C110", "D351", "D352"),
  gva      = c(120, 80, 45, 300, 150)
)

ind <- scale_from_leaftable(
  industries,
  frames = c("section", "division", "class"),
  weights = "gva",
  name   = "nace"
)

ind
#> NestedScale: nace
#> Frames (3, coarsest first):
#>   - section (2)
#>     - division (3)
#>       - class (5)
#> Leaves: 5
#> Weights: gva (default: gva)

Every structural question is answered from the leaves, never from an assumed tree:

scale_frames(ind)
#> [1] "section"  "division" "class"
scale_members(ind, "division")
#> [1] "C10" "C11" "D35"
scale_nests(ind, "section", "division")
#> [1] TRUE

Hierarchies that cross-cut are normal and supported – one detailed code may belong to several aggregates. scale_nests(x, parent, child) tests whether every child code belongs to a single parent code; conversion never depends on that relationship.

summary(ind)
#> <summary of NestedScale 'nace'>
#>   frames:         section (2) / division (3) / class (5)
#>   leaves:         5
#>   weight totals:  gva = 695  (default: gva)
#>   nesting:        section > division: nested
#>   nesting:        division > class: nested

Moving data between frames

Data keyed at one frame is recast to another with a rule per value column. With complete coverage, "sum" conserves totals; intensive quantities use "weighted_mean" with a declared weight:

x <- data.frame(
  class = c("C101", "C102", "C110", "D351", "D352"),
  jobs  = c(12, 8, 5, 30, 20),
  wage  = c(31, 29, 27, 45, 40)
)

recast_scale(x, ind, source = "class", target = "section",
             rule = c(jobs = "sum", wage = "weighted_mean"),
             weight = "gva")
#>   section jobs     wage
#> 1       C   25 29.61224
#> 2       D   50 43.33333

The same on time

Time is a dimension like any other: minutes group into hours, hours into days. The scale below has two days of 24 hours of 60 minutes, one row per minute, and a count per minute is summed to hours and to days.

grid <- expand.grid(m = 0:59, h = 0:23, d = 1:2)
clock <- data.frame(
  day    = sprintf("d%d", grid$d),
  hour   = sprintf("d%d_h%02d", grid$d, grid$h),
  minute = sprintf("d%d_h%02d_m%02d", grid$d, grid$h, grid$m)
)
time <- scale_from_leaftable(clock, frames = c("day", "hour", "minute"),
                             name = "clock")

visitors <- data.frame(minute = clock$minute, visitors = grid$h %/% 6 + 1)
head(recast_scale(visitors, time, source = "minute", target = "hour",
                  rule = "sum"), 3)
#>     hour visitors
#> 1 d1_h00       60
#> 2 d1_h01       60
#> 3 d1_h02       60
recast_scale(visitors, time, source = "minute", target = "day",
             rule = "sum")
#>   day visitors
#> 1  d1     3600
#> 2  d2     3600

This is only the bare mechanism. timescales builds on it for calendars with real dates, time zones, months of unequal length and typical or sampled periods.

Definition files and attributes

Scales travel as definition files (a JSON header with the tables inline, or a bundle with Arrow or CSV tables) that the Python binding reads as well. A scale may also carry values that belong to its members, such as the persons per household of a city, and alternative names for them. The values below are invented.

places <- attach_attributes_scale(
  places,
  data.frame(frame = c("region", "city"), member = c("N1", "e"),
             attribute = "hh_size", kind = "property", value = c(2.5, 2),
             unit_of_measure = "persons/household"),
  source = "example"
)
places <- attach_aliases_scale(
  places,
  data.frame(frame = "city", member = "a", alias = "Alder"),
  source = "example"
)
file <- tempfile(fileext = ".json")
write_scale(places, file)
places <- read_scale(file)
places
#> NestedScale: places
#> Frames (3, coarsest first):
#>   - country (2)
#>     - region (3)
#>       - city (7)
#> Leaves: 7
#> Attributes: hh_size (sources: example) -- 1 at region, 1 at city
#> Aliases: 1 (example)

households <- convert_scale(people[c(1, 2, 5), ], places, "hh_size",
                            from_unit = "persons", to_unit = "household")
names(households)[names(households) == "people"] <- "households"
households
#>   city households hh_size hh_size.origin_frame
#> 1    a        1.2     2.5               region
#> 2    b        0.8     2.5               region
#> 3    e        3.0     2.0                 city

scale_match(places, c("Alder", "B", "Zed"))
#>   label frame member method candidates
#> 1 Alder  city      a  alias       <NA>
#> 2     B  city      b  exact       <NA>
#> 3   Zed  <NA>   <NA>   none       <NA>

scale_attributes() resolves a value for every member of a frame, walking to the nearest coarser frame that holds one, so the cities a and b take the household size of their region. With the people counted in thousands, the converted column holds thousands of households. scale_match() resolves names and codes through the alias table, strictly.

Design

  • A scale is a definition, not a container. It holds the leaves, the frames that group them and the weights that size them. Data stays in ordinary tables and is matched to a scale by its codes; the experimental bind_scale() can also record on the code columns which scale and frame they are on.
  • Leaves are the ground truth. Frames are partitions of the leaves, not necessarily a strict tree; conversion always routes through the leaf layer.
  • Weights are named and plural. A scale can carry gva, employment and count side by side, with one declared default.
  • Attributes are not weights. A weight says how big a leaf is and drives aggregation; an attribute is a per-member factor, consumed row by row and never summed.
  • Partial coverage is first class. A leaf with no code at a frame is NA, not an error, and a subset records what fraction of its parent it keeps.
  • Backend-agnostic. The verbs use the dplyr interface, so the same pipeline runs on a data.frame, a data.table, or an arrow dataset; lazy inputs stay lazy.

Related packages

  • scales maps data to graphical aesthetics; its discrete scales are palettes and label formatters, not resolutions of a model dimension.
  • data.tree represents strict trees as node objects. nestedscales keeps the hierarchy as a flat leaf table, allows frames that cross-cut, and converts data between any two frames with weights.
  • hts reconciles forecasts across a fixed aggregation tree; reconcile_scale() here compares data aggregated with sum or weighted_mean against independent totals and can balance discrepancies.
